analysis.one_liner: Requires public companies to get shareholder approval before spending money on politics, and to disclose it.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee approved the bill 35–28 and it was placed on the House calendar on September 22, 2010, but it never received a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: After the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision opened the door to unlimited corporate spending in elections, this bill would have flipped that spending decision back to the company's owners. Public companies would need approval from a majority of their shareholders before spending money on elections, and directors would have to vote publicly on any political expenditure over $50,000. Every expenditure would be reported quarterly in searchable public records, and executives who spent money without approval could be sued by shareholders for three times the amount. The bill cleared the House Financial Services Committee 35–28 and was set on the House calendar, but no floor vote was ever scheduled.
analysis.who_benefits: Shareholders of public companies — which includes tens of millions of ordinary people through pensions, 401(k)s, and mutual funds — would gain a vote and full public disclosure of how their companies spend money on elections. Voters and the public generally would gain a searchable record of corporate political spending, including money routed through trade associations. Managers who chose to divest from politically active companies would gain legal protection for that choice.

how_it_helps.text: Shareholders — most of them ordinary people investing through pension funds and mutual funds — would vote on whether the company they part-own may spend money on politics, and their investment managers would have to disclose how they voted.

The public would get quarterly reports of every political expenditure, searchable and downloadable on the SEC's website, plus 48-hour public posting of the individual board votes authorizing each expenditure over $50,000.
Directors who spent corporate money on politics without shareholder approval would be personally liable to shareholders for three times the amount, giving the rule real teeth.
Investment managers who divested from companies because of their political spending would be shielded from lawsuits based solely on that decision.

analysis.who_pays: Publicly traded companies and their boards and executives: they would bear the cost of running shareholder votes, quarterly reporting, and board votes on every $50,000+ political expenditure, they would lose unilateral control over political spending, and they would face personal liability of three times any unauthorized expenditure. Trade associations receiving corporate dues for political use would lose the anonymity of those payments.

drawbacks.text: The compliance burden was heavy: companies would have to run a shareholder vote on proposed political spending each year, hold a board vote on every $50,000+ expenditure, publish director votes within 48 hours, and file quarterly reports listing each expenditure, the candidate involved, and the trade groups receiving corporate dues.

Directors who authorized political spending without shareholder approval would be personally liable to shareholders for three times the amount spent, which critics could reasonably call an invitation to litigation and a deterrent to any corporate participation in elections.

The bill exempted direct lobbying through registered lobbyists, so the most established and often most consequential channel of corporate influence in Washington would have remained outside shareholder approval and disclosure.

Requiring approval by a majority of all outstanding shares is a very high bar: with dispersed ownership and routine abstentions, even spending a broad majority of actual voters approved could be blocked.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For shareholders and voters, the benefits were large and concrete: a real vote and full, searchable disclosure over a channel of political spending that after Citizens United was nearly invisible, with treble damages to give the rule teeth. The costs were real too: significant compliance work for every listed company, a very high approval bar (a majority of all outstanding shares, where abstentions count against) that could paralyze political spending rather than just inform it, and litigation risk for directors. The design also had a glaring hole — it left direct lobbying through registered lobbyists untouched, which is often the largest and least visible channel of corporate influence in Washington. A stronger bill would have covered lobbying and used a lower, clearer approval threshold.

outcome.mechanism: The committee approved it and it was set on the House calendar in late September 2010, but no vote was ever scheduled before the session ended, and a bill left on the calendar dies when the new Congress begins.

narrative.text: Introduced March 9, 2010, the bill went to the Financial Services Committee, which approved it 35–28 on July 29, 2010, and reported it in amended form on September 22, 2010.
The same day, the House Administration Committee was discharged and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, the list of bills awaiting a floor vote.
No floor vote ever occurred, and the bill died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate boards and executives keep sole control of company political spending with no shareholder vote and no public disclosure, and the trade associations that receive their dues keep that money out of public view.

for.name: Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Shareholder Protection Act of 2010 in the House.

for.name: Barney Frank
for.what_they_did: Signed on as a sponsor and shepherded the bill through his committee, which approved it 35–28 and reported it to the House.

for.name: 49 of 254 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every cosponsor was a Democrat.

against.name: House Democratic leadership under Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor after it was placed on the calendar on September 22, 2010, less than two months before the November midterm election.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Opposed post-Citizens United measures requiring shareholder approval and public disclosure of corporate political spending.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors were Democrats and the committee's 35–28 vote to advance the bill split the committee's parties; the bill never reached the floor for a recorded vote that would show the full split.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: Boards and executives would lose unilateral control over corporate political spending, face quarterly disclosure and 48-hour publication of board votes, and risk personal liability of three times any unauthorized expenditure. The bill died, so they keep sole discretion and no public disclosure.

industries.industry: Trade associations and tax-exempt groups funded by corporate dues
industries.note: Payments to trade associations or other nonprofits that could be used for campaign ads or electioneering would have to be named and disclosed, closing the common route companies used to influence elections anonymously. The bill's death keeps that route open.

industries.industry: Institutional investment managers (mutual funds, asset managers)
industries.note: They would take on a new duty to disclose how they voted on corporate political spending, but in exchange the bill gave them a legal safe harbor to divest from companies over their politics without being sued. Their gain and burden roughly offset.

The bill explicitly exempted direct lobbying by registered lobbyists from the shareholder-approval and disclosure rules, so lobbying would remain the compliant, unpoliced channel of corporate influence while independent campaign spending was restricted. That carve-out survived only on paper since the bill never became law.
